payload.title: Bringing the River Back
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, a stream running through a growing city was treated as a drain. It was straightened, lined with concrete and finally buried, and the ground above it became a road or a car park. The logic was simple: water that could not be seen could not flood, could not smell, and could not be blamed for disease. Whole rivers disappeared from the maps in this way, surviving only in the names of the streets laid over them.

The reversal, known as daylighting, began where the engineering had failed rather than where the nostalgia was strongest. Buried culverts age badly, and replacing a collapsing concrete tunnel beneath a city centre can cost more than removing it altogether and letting the stream run in the open air. Seoul's Cheonggyecheon, uncovered in 2005 once the elevated motorway above it was judged unsafe, is the example everyone cites, but smaller schemes in Sheffield, Zurich and Yonkers were driven by the same unglamorous arithmetic.

What the engineers did not anticipate was how much else would change. An open channel slows heavy rain instead of firing it downstream, so flooding fell in districts the project had never been designed to protect, and summer temperatures beside the water dropped by two or three degrees. Property values rose as well, and that is where the difficulty begins: the residents who lived for decades with the culvert are not always the ones who can afford the street once the river is back.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Cities are uncovering their buried streams mainly because the ageing culverts have become expensive to maintain, and the finished projects have delivered benefits nobody planned for along with a new problem of affordability.
Daylighting has been driven above all by public affection for lost rivers, which is why the schemes started in the cities with the longest recorded history.
Burying urban streams was recognised as an engineering mistake from the beginning, and nineteenth-century critics correctly predicted that it would make flooding worse.
Seoul's Cheonggyecheon is the only daylighting scheme that has ever worked, and other cities have quietly abandoned the idea as too costly.

payload.title: What the Forest Floor Actually Does
paragraphs: Few scientific images have travelled as far as the wood wide web. Fungal threads, the story goes, knit the roots of a forest into a single network along which older trees feed sugar to struggling seedlings, and warnings of insect attack pass from neighbour to neighbour. The picture is attractive because it turns a wood into a community, and it has been repeated in documentaries, novels and school textbooks until it reads like settled fact.

The underlying biology is not in doubt. Mycorrhizal fungi genuinely wrap around and enter tree roots, and they genuinely trade mineral nutrients for the sugars a tree makes above ground; carbon labelled in a laboratory has certainly been traced from one seedling into another through fungal tissue. What is disputed is the leap from those observations to the claim that mature trees deliberately support their offspring. A recent review of the field found that the most-cited studies were small, conducted mostly in a handful of North American plots, and rarely repeated.

The correction matters beyond the seminar room. Forestry policies have been redrafted on the assumption that leaving a few large trees standing will nurse a new generation through the network below, and money has followed the assumption. If the transfers are modest, or if the fungus is simply pursuing its own interest rather than the forest's, the practice may still be worth keeping for other reasons, but the reasons will have to be argued rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: The fungal connections between forest trees are real, but the popular claim that old trees deliberately nurse seedlings through them rests on thin evidence, which matters because forestry policy has already been built on it.
Mycorrhizal fungi have turned out not to exist in the form biologists once described, and the entire field will have to begin again from the laboratory.
Documentaries and novels should be barred from discussing scientific findings until those findings have been replicated by independent teams.
Because trees clearly cooperate underground, forestry policy has at last caught up with what ecologists have known for a century.
